title: Timelapse (rotating supercell thunderstorm)
date: 2019-07-19 (Flickr posting date; date taken not recorded)
place: Great Plains, USA (exact location not given on the page)
notes: Time-lapse of a huge rotating supercell ('mothership' shape) with banded, striated cloud layers over flat fields, with lightning flicks under the storm. The source is only 12 s long and letterboxed (1420x1080 with black bars, active area 1420x948), so this file is two pieces joined: source 0-3.7 s (wide view over a bare field, storm centre x~0.45) and source 5.25-12 s (low view down a dirt road, the storm rotating right above, centre x~0.5), cropped to 1420x798 (16:9, y offset 150), upscaled to 1920x1080, and SLOWED to 0.771x speed with blended frame interpolation (ffmpeg framerate filter) so the file lasts 13.53 s instead of 14. The scene change is at about 4.8 s in this file. Source 3.7-5.2 s was left out on purpose: it is a short different shot with four people launching a weather balloon. Best seconds: 4.8-13.5 (dirt-road view, most dramatic rotation). Small power poles at the far right edge. No people, no text, no logos in this cut.
fact_en: NOAA Storm Prediction Center: 'Supercells often produce damaging wind, large hail, and tornadoes, and most strong to violent tornadoes are associated with supercells.' Their rotating updraft 'is known as a mesocyclone'.
